title: Mints with the Bill
text:
Restaurants often bring a mint or a piece of chocolate with the bill. In 2002 David Strohmetz, Bruce Rind, Reed Fisher and Michael Lynn published experiments testing whether this small gift changes how much diners tip.

In their studies, carried out in restaurants in the United States, servers delivered the bill in different ways, decided in advance for each table. Some diners got no candy. Some got one piece of chocolate per person with the check. Some got two pieces. In a fourth condition, the server first left one piece per person, started to walk away, then turned back and offered each diner a second piece, as if on a sudden personal impulse.

Tips rose with the gift. A single piece of candy raised them only slightly, about 3 percent. Two pieces raised them by about 14 percent. But the largest increase, about 23 percent, came when the server returned with the second piece. The diners received the same amount of chocolate in both two-piece conditions. What changed was the impression that the extra gift was personal, unexpected and meant for them, which turned a routine courtesy into a small act of kindness that diners wanted to repay.
lesson: How a kindness is given matters as much as what is given. A small gesture that feels personal and unexpected means more than a bigger routine one.
people: David Strohmetz, Bruce Rind, Reed Fisher, Michael Lynn
source: Strohmetz, D. B., Rind, B., Fisher, R., and Lynn, M. (2002). Sweetening the till: The use of candy to increase restaurant tipping. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 32(2), 300-309.
